title: Mustard Seed
tagline: Sunday readings and activities for Catholic families, in English and Spanish.
headline: I built Mustard Seed for my kids. So why did I stop?
summary: I built Mustard Seed so my kids could understand Sunday Mass. It was my first app built with AI: an iOS app, an admin and a marketing site on one Supabase backend, in English and Spanish. I stopped after a few weeks, and what I heard from parents became Pause.
outcomes: My first app built with AI, from Figma to the App Store
Three sides on one backend: an iOS app, an admin and a marketing site, in English and Spanish
Parents told me they don't hand phones to kids at Mass. That idea became Pause

beats.headline: Why I built it
beats.body:
When I took my kids to Mass, they didn't do much besides roam around or play little games on my phone. I wanted to bring them closer to my faith, and I wanted to go over the readings with them before and after, in words a five-year-old and a three-year-old could follow.

So I built Mustard Seed. It started as a personal project, but my intention was always to see if it was marketable and if I could sell it.

beats.headline: My first app built with AI
beats.body:
This was my first attempt at building anything with AI. I used Cursor with Xcode, and I took it all the way to the App Store.

I didn't have the Figma MCP, and I wasn't using Claude Code yet. I gave the tools a Figma link and Figma screenshots. Even then, the app came out almost exactly the way I'd designed it, down to how it feels. I thought, wow, I can do these things now.

beats.headline: Finding the look
beats.body:
I started by imagining a purple and mustard brand. I did a couple of runs, and the more I looked at it, the less I felt it. It was heavy and drastic. I wanted something clean and simple.

I also realized that parents would be the ones using this most, even though it was for kids. So I went with a muted yellow and a darker green, and built the splash screen from that.

beats.body: I did my usual first pass, the happy path: what the app looks like when everything goes right, what it will have, how it should feel. After that I built it.

beats.headline: What the app does
beats.body:
You come in on Sunday and read the First Reading, the Second Reading and the Gospel with your kids, in a format they can understand. Each week, they can also complete an activity.

- This Sunday: the readings for the week, written for kids
- Past Sundays: an archive to go back to
- Activities: a coloring page, a maze, and a word search
- The seed: it grows a little every Sunday

image.caption: This Sunday's readings, plus past weeks

beats.headline: The seed
beats.body:
Progress is displayed as a growing mustard seed. There are 8 stages, and every Sunday the seed grows a bit closer to bloom. It starts to sprout vegetables.

The idea was that you'd see your progress as the weeks went by. It's gentle. There are no streaks to feel bad about, just a plant that gets bigger.

image.caption: The seed growing across the weeks

beats.headline: The word search
beats.body:
The word search is where my puzzle idea started. It was the first time I tried one, and I thought, whoa, it would be cool to have puzzle-like things inside an app so kids could be entertained.

The puzzle is dynamic: it brings in words from that week's reading. That's the idea that later turned into the puzzles in Pause.

image.caption: The word search, built from that week's reading

beats.headline: Content every week
beats.body:
If the app was going to be live, it was going to need new content every week. I couldn't ship an App Store update every Sunday, so the content had to live outside the app.

So I built an admin website using Supabase as a backend. A Sunday shows up in the app once its publish date passes, and I could schedule weeks ahead.

beats.headline: English and Spanish
beats.body:
I speak Spanish with my kids, and my kids mainly speak Spanish, so I knew I wanted the app in at least two languages.

It was also my first time localizing an app. Spanish is longer. "Start free trial" becomes "Comenzar prueba gratuita", which is a very long message. Seeing how that stretched the UI was a great lesson.

image.caption: Comenzar prueba gratuita, the Spanish for Start free trial

beats.headline: Too much to keep up with
beats.body:
I updated content myself for a couple of weeks. Then I realized it was going to be very hard to keep up.

Every week I had to retell the readings in simple words, in English and in Spanish, make an image for each reading, and think of an activity. I wasn't going to have the time to do that week after week.

beats.headline: Did anyone want it?
beats.body:
Mustard Seed was a personal project, but I still wanted to see if other people were interested. I went out and searched Reddit and joined Facebook groups.

The feedback was loud. Parents don't give phones to kids at Mass. They give them books. And they're adamantly against screen time.

image.caption: What parents told me on Reddit and in Facebook groups

beats.body:
In the end I stopped supporting the app and stopped posting the readings. I wrote to the few users I had, six people, and apologized. They all understood where I was coming from.

It went nowhere as a product. But it planted a seed - no pun intended. People really are against screen time, and that's what I later went on to solve with Pause.

beats.body:
- I can build things with AI now.
- I can try to market them, too. Building was only half of it, and this is probably the hardest hurdle.
- Designing for content is design work.
- Language changes the UI. Spanish is longer than English, so I design for the longer word.
- Small projects teach the most.

article:
When I took my kids to Mass, they didn't do much besides roam around or play little games on my phone. I wanted to bring them closer to my faith, and I wanted to go over the readings with them before and after, in words a five-year-old and a three-year-old could follow. So I built Mustard Seed.

It started as a personal project, but my intention was always to see if it was marketable and if I could sell it. It was also the first time I wondered whether I could build something with AI, so I tried it with Cursor and Xcode, all the way to the App Store. Mustard Seed felt nice and safe enough to learn on.

I stopped publishing it after a few weeks. This is what I built, why I stopped, and what it taught me, including the seed that became Pause.

**Tools:** Figma, Cursor, Xcode, Supabase, Next.js, Netlify

## 1. Why I built it

The idea was simple. My kids and I go to church, and they didn't have a lot to do there. I wanted to give them activities, and a way to review what the readings were about, written so a five-year-old and a three-year-old could understand.

![The readings, written for adults](content/mustard-seed/readings-adults.png)

## 2. My first app built with AI

This was my first attempt at building anything with AI. I used Cursor with Xcode, and I took it all the way to the App Store.

I didn't have the Figma MCP, and I wasn't using Claude Code yet. I gave the tools a Figma link and Figma screenshots. Even then, the app came out almost exactly the way I'd designed it, down to how it feels. That was an enlightening moment. I thought, wow, I can do these things now.

## 3. Finding the look

I started by imagining a purple and mustard brand. Purple contrasts really well with mustard, and I wanted to emulate that. I did a couple of runs, and the more I looked at it, the less I felt it. It was heavy and drastic. I wanted something clean and simple.

I also realized that parents would be the ones using this most, even though it was for kids. So I went with a muted yellow and a darker green, and built the splash screen from that.

![The purple and mustard direction I dropped](content/mustard-seed/purple-direction.webp)

![The splash screen: a muted yellow wordmark on dark green with a subtle gradient](content/mustard-seed/splash.png)

Then I did my usual first pass, the happy path: what the app looks like when everything goes right, what it will have, how it should feel. After that I built it.

![The happy path: every screen in the first pass, with everything going right](content/mustard-seed/happy-path.webp)

![Giving design feedback while iterating on the dark mode](content/mustard-seed/dark-mode-feedback.webp)

## 4. What the app does

You come in on Sunday and read the First Reading, the Second Reading and the Gospel with your kids, in a format they can understand. Each week, they can also complete an activity.

- **This Sunday:** the readings for the week, written for kids
- **Past Sundays:** an archive to go back to
- **Activities:** a coloring page you color on the iPad, a maze, and a word search
- **The seed:** it grows a little every Sunday

![This Sunday's readings, plus past weeks](content/mustard-seed/app.jpg)

### The seed

Progress is displayed as a growing mustard seed. There are 8 stages, and every Sunday the seed grows a bit closer to bloom. It starts to sprout vegetables. The idea was that you'd see your progress as the weeks went by. It's gentle. There are no streaks to feel bad about, just a plant that gets bigger.

![The seed growing across the weeks](content/mustard-seed/seed-growing.webp)

### The word search

The word search is where my puzzle idea started. It was the first time I tried one, and I thought, whoa, it would be cool to have puzzle-like things inside an app so kids could be entertained. The puzzle is dynamic: it brings in words from that week's reading. That's the idea that later turned into the puzzles in Pause.

![The word search, built from that week's reading](content/mustard-seed/word-search.png)

## 5. Content every week

If the app was going to be live, it was going to need new content every week. I couldn't ship an App Store update every Sunday, so the content had to live outside the app. That meant a server-side CMS where I could get the readings for the next Sunday, turn them into kid-friendly words, and paste them in, so anyone opening the app would see it updated.

So I built an admin website using Supabase as a backend. A Sunday shows up in the app once its publish date passes, and I could schedule weeks ahead.

I updated content myself for a couple of weeks. Then I realized it was going to be very hard to keep up. Every week I had to retell the readings in simple words, make an image for each reading, and think of an activity. I wasn't going to have the time to do that week after week.

## 6. English and Spanish

I speak Spanish with my kids, and my kids mainly speak Spanish, so I knew I wanted the app in at least two languages. That meant the admin needed an English side and a Spanish side, where I'd put in both versions of everything.

It turned into a lot of work. Every Sunday I had to bring in the readings, cite the scripture that was indicated, write it all in English and in Spanish, and bring the activity in and explain it in Spanish too.

It was also my first time localizing an app, and it showed me how much language matters in the copy and in the buttons. Spanish is longer. "Start free trial" becomes "Comenzar prueba gratuita", which is a very long message. Seeing how that stretched the UI was a great lesson.

![Comenzar prueba gratuita, the Spanish for Start free trial](content/mustard-seed/spanish-trial.webp)

## 7. Did anyone want it?

Mustard Seed was a personal project, but I still wanted to see if other people were interested. It had three sides: the app, the admin, and a marketing site where I wrote blog posts to bring in traffic. I also went out and searched Reddit and joined Facebook groups.

The feedback was loud. Parents don't give phones to kids at Mass. They give them books. And they're adamantly against screen time.

![What parents told me on Reddit and in Facebook groups](content/mustard-seed/reddit-feedback.png)

## 8. Stopping

In the end I stopped supporting the app and stopped posting the readings. I wrote to the few users I had, six people, and apologized. I told them what was up and that I wouldn't be maintaining it. They all understood where I was coming from.

It went nowhere as a product. But it planted a seed - no pun intended. What I'd heard from those parents told me something I could build on: people really are against screen time, and once you start looking into it, there's an actual problem there. That's what I later went on to solve with Pause.

## 9. What I learned

- **I can build things with AI now.** My vision came out at almost 100% fidelity from a Figma link and screenshots, without the Figma MCP or Claude Code.
- **I can try to market them, too.** Building was only half of it, and this is probably the hardest hurdle.
- **Designing for content is design work.** Workflows, an admin, and a weekly schedule all needed to be designed.
- **Language changes the UI.** Spanish is longer than English, so I design for the longer word.
- **Small projects teach the most.** It went nowhere, but it taught me a lot, and that things are possible.

## Deep dives

### The three sides

Mustard Seed has three parts that all read from one Supabase backend.

- **The iOS app:** what families use
- **The marketing site:** readings, activities and a blog, built to bring in traffic and downloads
- **The admin site:** a dashboard of drafts and published weeks, a Sunday editor, uploads for images and PDFs, and schedule and publish

Each Sunday reading consists of four readings (First Reading, Psalm, Second Reading, Gospel) with English and Spanish titles, summaries and references, plus one activity and a publish date. Only people on the admin list can sign in, and row-level security enforces it in the database.

### The build

- **iOS:** Swift and SwiftUI, StoreKit 2 for subscriptions and a free trial, PencilKit for coloring on activities
- **Offline:** a local cache with background refresh
- **Web and admin:** Next.js on Netlify
- **Backend:** Supabase for auth, Postgres, and storage for images and PDFs

### A hidden admin mode

The app has its own hidden admin entry: triple-tap the version number in Settings. It has drafts, an editor, and a Seed Growth Emulator to preview how the seed looks as it grows.

Sound familiar? You found this editor the same way.
